speechtext:
On
a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, on my return to the city early last week I was twitted by a number of hon. members with

Farmers' Creditors Act
regard to certain things I am alleged to have said during the progress of the Saskatchewan election. Although I searched diligently for it, I could not until Wednesday afternoon locate in Hansard what the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) had charged me with saying. I would have brought it to your attention yesterday, but out of deference to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) who was presenting his budget I deferred doing so until to-day.
I find on reference to Hansard of June 7 last at page 3619 the following:
Mr. Chevrier:	I am sure your government
would satisfy the hungry people.
Mr. Bennett: Do not let us talk about hunger. Just think of it! One hon. member, not here, saying that if you be hungry in Saskatchewan do not think of voting for this government. Do not think of voting for this government. If you be hungry think what will happen if you do not vote for the Patterson government. That is what the hon. member for Regina (Mr. McNiven) has been stating to the people of this country, according to the public press.
I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, and other hon. members, that I never said anything, either directly or indirectly, which by any stretch of imagination could be so construed. What is more, I have diligently searched the Regina press, and I cannot find any reference therein that could be so construed.
Again on June 9, as reported in Hansard on page 3700, I find these statements in an address by the right hon. leader of the opposition:
And we have those who are responsible for providing the relief telling them that if they do not vote Liberal they will be hungry.
As a result of that statement the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) asked the leader of the opposition this question:
Will the right hon. leader of the opposition give the committee the name of a single individual who stated to any one that unless he voted in a certain way he would go hungry?
Mr. Bennett:	The hon. member for Regina
City is reported in the press to have said that the reason why the electors of Saskatchewan should return Liberal candidates in that province in yesterday's election was that they had obtained more money than they would have obtained if there had not been a Liberal government there and a Liberal government here.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I deny absolutely that I made any suggestion that any money had been obtained by the people of Saskatchewan, either through the provincial or through the dominion government, other than that -which was necessary by reason of the disaster which had befallen that province.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved:
That a message be sent to the Senate acquainting their honours that this house disagrees to their amendments to Bill No. 25, an act to amend the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, 1934, for the following reason:
Because the adoption of the said amendments would impose hardship in certain provinces.
And that the clerk do carry the said message to the Senate.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does that apply to all
the amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, I will explain. The amendment to which exception is taken is an amendment to the last section of the bill as it left this house, section 8, an amendment which provided as follows:
On and after a date to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council, no new proposal shall be made or filed by any farmer or accepted by any official receiver in any province in respect of which the said proclamation is issued.
That was as the bill left this house. But coming back from the senate a new section 9 is added which provides to the following effect:
The said act is further amended by adding to section eleven, as subsection three, the following:
No proposal shall be received in any province later than the thirty-first day of December, 1938, except in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the senate amendment. The effect of it, of course, is to end the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act at the end of this year in all provinces except Saskatchewan and Alberta.
The view of the government is that it is not at all certain at this time that in all the other provinces the Farmers' Creditors
Farmers' Creditors Act

Arrangement Act should go out of business, so far as new applications are concerned, on the 31st of December of this year. The government, and I as Minister of Finance, have received representations from people in some of the other provinces that this would be unduly arbitrary so far as they are concerned, and I think that may be said particularly in respect of Manitoba. The discussion of this motion might serve to reveal the views of representatives of other provinces concerned, as to the desirability of arbitrarily terminating the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act at the end of the year in all provinces except Saskatchewan and Alberta. The view of the government is that we should disagree with the amendment.

It is probable, as the minister has said, that the executive would be better able to exercise the discretion than would this parliament with respect to any particular province, and I would concur in the message to their honours if the motion be amended so as to make it clear that it applies only to section 9 of the bill.

I should like, however, an expression of view from hon. members from other provinces who may take exception to this senate amendment.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased indeed that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has indicated that the government intends to oppose the amendment .made to this bill by the senate. So far as I know, no representations have been made on behalf of anyone in the province of British Columbia that the operation of the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act should cease in that province at the end of this year. I was surprised that the amendment should have been moved by someone who had no interest whatever in British Columbia and had received no representations from that province, when the effect of the amendment is to leave British Columbia outside the operation of the act after the end of this year. The amendment would certainly work a great hardship not only on certain farmers but particularly on the soldier settlers, who we were told this year, would have the opportunity of going before the board under this act with a view to receiving an adjustment. I protest against the senate amendment, and I am glad that the minister has moved non-concurrence.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from statements made in this house and representations made from various parts of Ontario I believe it would meet with the approval of the province of Ontario if the act were discontinued so far as Ontario is concerned. Quite a number of members from Ontario spoke on this bill when it was before the house, and almost all of them, if not all, were in favour of having the act discontinued in respect to Ontario.
It occurred to me that instead of sending the message to the senate in the form suggested it might be possible to change the wording of the bill

I am making not a motion but merely a suggestion-to make it read that no new proposals shall be received in the province of Ontario after the 31st of December, 1938.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has said, that this house should refuse to accept the amendment made by the senate. I know there are arguments pro and con respecting the continued operation of this legislation in Manitoba, but there has been no crystallized opinion in that province against the continuance of the act, and now that the question is before the house I submit that Manitoba itself should have the right to say whether the legislation should be dropped so far as that province is concerned. I am quite sure I speak for many in Manitoba when I say that

Farmers' Creditors Act
the Manitoba legislature is the proper authority to cancel the operation of the act, and until that has been done I entirely agree with the Minister of Finance.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I heartily endorse the action taken by the Minister of Finance in rejecting the amendment made by the senate, I would call attention to a phase that has not been mentioned by previous speakers. At page 2710 of Hansard of May 9, when the minister was putting through this bill, I called his attention to the fact that-
*-the opportunities of this act were largely relied upon by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) when he was putting through the amendment to the Soldier Settlement Act.
We asked him again and again what the soldier settler was going to do without an extension of the dollar for dollar bonus provision that we were asking for, and he replied that they could get relief under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. I called the attention of the Minister of Finance to that and asked him to give his assurance that he would look into it before he made, any decision, at least as regards British Columbia, and he did give that assurance. I may say I heard no suggestion that it should be done away with in British Columbia, and certainly, if it is done away with, one would expect in all good faith that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) would introduce amendments to the Soldier Settlement Act giving us an extension on the dollar for dollar bonus.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext: I understood that for some time the British Columbia government has been opposed to this legislation, and no doubt any information which the other house acted upon came from that source. Without doubt there have been complaints. At the same time I think we agree that this legislation has done a lot of good, in relieving many of the farmers in our province. However it cannot continue very much longer, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has been wise in proceeding as he has, and in providing that it shall be left to the governor in council, who would be in a better position than this house to ascertain at what period the legislation should be withdrawn from British Columbia or any other province.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I heartily agree with the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) that so far as Ontario is concerned we should like to see the act discontinued. I was in the house when this
act passed, and we were assured it was to be a temporary measure, to give temporary relief to people who had purchased land in war time, when prices were very high, and had borrowed money at a high rate. They have now had four years to make these adjustments, and I should like to see this act wiped off the statute books. Any statute which interferes with a legitimate contract is dangerous legislation, and this act has interfered with legitimate contracts between borrowers and lenders. The government may have had some justification for entering upon this course four years ago, when farmers were paying high rates of interest and when it was thought desirable to adjust some sales of land which had been made at exorbitant prices. But they have had time to make, these adjustments. I think the act has fulfilled its usefulness and should be discontinued.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This gives me an opportunity to repeat what I have said on former occasions in connection with this act. As has been stated by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson), it was intended to be a temporary measure. Moreover the act has application only to debts contracted before it was passed, which was in the year 1935; so that any debt contracted by a farmer since 1935 does not come under its provisions. Surely three years is a sufficient time within which debts contracted prior to 1935 could be brought to an adjustment under the provisions of this act. I believe that most of the farmers who can come under the act with respect to debts prior to 1935 have done so; at least they have had their opportunity, and if notice is now published and given to them that the end of 1938 will be the limit of the act, they will have had ample time to come in.
I regard it as in the public interest that the act should be terminated, and I think it ought to be definitely known when it will be terminated. Let us remove the uncertainty about it. I do not care to speak for any province other than my own, but in Ontario the sentiment is overwhelmingly in favour of immediate termination. I had hoped that the minister would end it by the first of July, but of course that cannot be done, under the provisions of this measure, until it passes. I still hope that he will take the very first opportunity to proclaim the termination of the act in its application to the province of Ontario.

subtopic: BOARDS OF REVIEW, TIME LIMIT FOR FILING PROPOSALS, ETC.-NON-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENT
speechtext:
With reference to what the last two speakers have said. I am glad indeed to know that
Northioest Territories Act

the act so far as the province of Saskatchewan is concerned is not to be interfered with, and I thoroughly concur in what the Senate and the House of Commons have agreed upon, namely, to leave the act, so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, still in operation. Certain portions of the province of Saskatchewan, over fifty per cent of its area, have not had a crop for nine years. How is it possible to go in there at the present time and adjust debts? The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in those portions of the province has not even begun to operate. It is impossible to value land which has had no crop for nine years. No one can say what it is worth. Only after we have some crops-and we hope we shall have crops from now on-will it be possible to put the act in operation. So we are glad that the act is to remain operative so far as Saskatchewan is concerned.

maintopic: AMENDMENT BESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the senate to Bill No. 110, to amend the Northwest Territories Act.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: AMENDMENT BESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
This is really the preparation and submission to this house of an entirely new bill. It cannot in any sense be said to be a mere amendment. It proceeds on an entirely different theory from the legislation submitted to us in Bill No. 110. The bill contemplated the issue by the exchequer court of what is known technically as a writ of assistance. The senate has seen fit to draft a new bill, which provides that the Secretary of State may issue a certificate which has all the effects of a writ of assistance and is issued under the seal of the Secretary of State. After a cursory examination of it but taking some degree of care it would seem to me that from the standpoint of efficiency and effectiveness the senate's suggestion is probably a better one than ours. In every case it was contemplated to attend on the exchequer court and secure a writ of assistance. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) knows that a writ of assistance is something which is easily obtained but sometimes may be readily abused, and this gives the government complete control of the situa-

tion by the grant of a certificate the form of which is set out in the new statute, which contemplates that the certificate shall be issued only to some person in the public service of Canada and at the instance of His Majesty's Attorney General of Canada. To ask that we concur in the amendments means that we concur in an entirely new bill, with which I am not in disagreement at all, though I think it fair to point out that it is an entire departure from that which we commenced with when we considered Bill No. 110.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: AMENDMENT BESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman is
quite right. This is entirely different from what has been proposed in the bill introduced by the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), and it is also rather a change from what is usually done under similar circumstances. But we have carefully considered the change made by the senate amendment. Neither the officers of the Department of Justice nor those of the Department of the Secretary of State have any objection to the change, radical as it is, and under the circumstances I am quite willing, so far as I am concerned, to accept it, and concur in the amendment.

maintopic: AMENDMENT BESPECTING SHIPMENT OR TAKING OUT OF FURS WITHOUT PROPER AUTHORITY- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext:
Absolutely.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS

speechtext: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) moved the second reading of and concurrence in amendments made by the senate to Bill No. 98, respecting the North Pacific Pelagic Sealing convention.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
There are quite a number of amendments, but for the most part they consist in the striking out of certain sections of the bill, which brought in certain sections of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, bringing pelagic sealing under those sections. The senate has struck out those sections and substituted a sort of summary of them, and I should like to call attention to what is now proposed. I know that they have only followed the wording of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act,

Pelagic Sealing
but the fact that something is old does not necessarily mean that it is right, and if we never did correct anything on the ground that it was long established we would not make much progress. At page 456 of Votes and Proceedings the proposed amendment to subsection 2, of section 1 reads:
If the master or person in command of any such ship, vessel or boat does not, upon any examination under oath by any officer or person under the authority of this act touching the cargo, equipment and voyage of such ship, vessel or boat-
That is, any boat that has been boarded by the officials.
-truly answer all questions put to him in such examination, he shall incur a fine of $400.
I would point out first of all that the men concerned, who will be accused in these cases, will almost inevitably be Indians, because the bill is dealing with Indians who shoot or kill seals illegally. If they took ten seals in one day, which would be phenomenal, the total value would not exceed thirty or forty dollars; and for an offence involving the illegal shooting of forty dollars' worth of seals, these Indians will be liable to a fine of $400- that is, if they do not truly answer all questions under oath. Now, there is a criminal code in Canada and that code provides a certain penalty for perjury. That offence is dealt with by itself in the code and it is severe, and I cannot see why it is necessary to introduce into this act a part of the criminal code, setting it up independently of the code and putting it into operation.
Next it is proposed to insert the following as a new subsection (3) of section 11:
(3) Every person opposing any officer or person in the execution of his duty under this act or aiding or abetting any other person in such opposition is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a fine of $800 and to two years' imprisonment.
Section 4 of the bill as we passed it provided that under the circumstances here indicated the person contravening the regulation should be guilty of an offence against the act; and in section 11, as the bill passed this house, it was provided that every person guilty of an offence against the act or of a contravention of any regulation should be liable to a fine not exceeding $500 or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months; and that was upon summary conviction. It seems to me that what we provided in the bill originally was quite sufficient considering the essentially small value of the goods involved; but the other legislative body
has taken the matter out of the category of summary convictions and made it an indictable offence, imposing the enormous penalty of $800 and two years' imprisonment. That, I submit, is unjust. It is unfair to impose such a heavy penalty for an offence involving so small a matter as thirty dollars' worth of skins. Surely the provision in the bill as we passed it, making the offence subject to summary conviction, was the most workable one in these outlying places. Now, however, it is proposed to make the offence indictable, and the penalty as severe as I have indicated. I submit that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) might consider the wisdom of objecting to that amendment on the ground that it is unnecessarily severe.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
There is only one section
to which I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and that is the new section 13 which provides that the statutory limitations shall be three years. I submit that, having regard to the character of this legislation, twelve months would be ample time within which to institute proceedings. When we are dealing with a floating population, to have these matters stand over for as long as three years is sometimes, in my opinion, to do nothing but encourage what I once heard a learned judge describe as a species of blackmail, and I think three years may be a little long.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Is that
a provision added by the senate?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Yes. It reads:
All actions for the recovery or enforcement of penalties or forfeitures imposed by this act shall be commenced within three years after the offence committed.
I submit that one year is ample, but I merely express that view to the minister. So far as the other sections are concerned, there is no doubt that what the senate has done is to endeavour to make this a code within itself, by adding thereto, instead of leaving to inference, the provisions of a statute, namely, that dealing with violations of the customs act; and notwithstanding what my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said, I always think it is desirable to have within the four corners of a statute itself all provisions that have to do with the institution of proceedings and the recovery of penalties rather than leave them open to uncertainty and doubt. I am inclined to think
Pelagic Sealing

that the amendments made by the senate are an improvement in the legislation, but owing to the discussion that took place when the matter was before this chamber, and the indication by the minister that he wanted the matter treated in the way in which it was, we made the provisions of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act applicable without specifically indicating, as the senate has now done, the sections in question.
I am at variance with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni as to the severity of the penalty in connection with interference with officers in the discharge of their duties. I suppose the hon. gentleman would expect me to differ from him anyway, but it is one of the general principles of our jurisprudence that we cannot afford too great protection to those into whose hands we entrust the enforcement of laws in view of the fact that very often they risk their lives in carrying them out. I have a consistent record of endeavouring to ensure that, and therefore I must be at variance with my hon. friend and favour the amendments made by the senate.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is right in stating that what the senate did in this bill was to include the provisions that were there before only by inference. Section 3 of the bill as it left this house read:
Section five and all of the following sections, except sections ten and twenty-nine, of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, chapter forty-three of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, shall be deemed to apply, in so far as applicable, for all the purposes of this act, and shall have effect as if enacted herein.
The provisions of section 3 of the Customs and Fisheries Protection Act, and other sections referred to herein, have been included and have been made specifically part of this act. I believe this tends to make for greater clarity in administration, and especially is it better in view of the fact that the act is to be distributed in other countries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: That is the point.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SANCTIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF NORTH PACIFIC SEALING CONVENTION-CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Regarding the undue
severity of the penalty, may I say that the senate committee has not informed us of its reasons for maintaining them as they were; but inasmuch as there is no actual change from what was enacted in this chamber, we have been disposed to approve of and to accept the suggestions of the senate.
Motion agreed to; amendments read the second time and concurred in.

I did not know this bill would be discussed this afternoon. It had been my intention to go into the matter with the Minister of Finance, because some people fear that it would affect certain parts of the civil law of the province of Quebec. For instance, paragraph (e) reads as follows:
The loan shall be for such period and upon such terms as to payment of principal, interest and taxes by monthly instalments as the minister shall determine-
And so on. I believe there are other parts of the measure to the same effect. May I point out that according to the laws of the province of Quebec as contained in the civil code and other municipal legislation, municipal taxes, school taxes and church assessments
are privileged, and are paid before a first mortgage or any other imposition. In view of the wording of the section I wonder if the people in the province of Quebec are not justified in the fear that when the act says the money loaned by either the minister or a lending corporation shall be secured by a first mortgage, such mortgage will be privileged over church assessments, and municipal and school taxes. I should like to ask that some clarification of this and other sections be made, so as to allay the fears of people in my native province.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext: Paragraph (e) is worded in exactly the same way as the corresponding section of the Dominion Housing Act under which we have been operating for more than two years. I may point out at once that there is no intention, nor would it be valid if there was, to set the mortgage ahead of taxes. That could not be. The subsection merely intends, and has been so administered in the past, to enable the mortgage agreement to be dealt with by means of monthly payments. In some provinces, and in some connections, it is desirable to have the arrangement for monthly repayment of the loan also include a monthly contribution to be applied on the taxes, and so far as I can learn we have had no trouble in any province in working out that phase of it.

I do not see anything in the act which prohibits such action, but would the bill forbid the municipality or any local authority or lending company to sell such houses at any time after they are built, provided that certain conditions proposed by the minister have been complied with? I am interested to know that, having regard to the experience I had in municipal affairs some years ago. The committee will recall that we had federal legislation under which similar associations or companies built houses in municipalities and small towns and even in cities, and it was found to be a complete failure, a complete loss to the municipality. I have in mind municipalities which lost large amounts of money, over a million dollars. I do not want to compare municipalities with governments, but sometimes we find from experience that they are worse than the government as to their capacity to administer something that private individuals could administer. With a municipality administering houses in that way, the residents of the municipality generally believe that they are not bound to pay the rent, not bound to make repairs or pay for them. Sometimes they go further than that; they do not take care of the property at all, and the municipality generally speaking is in a very bad situation. So that unless there is some measure which forces the municipality to impose its city regulations upon the tenants, I do not believe it is a good thing. That is my personal view. That is why I am in some cases in favour of selling these properties to individuals. I believe it is a good policy to give facilities to municipalities to build these low cost houses, but at the same time I believe it would be good policy to facilitate the selling of these houses to reliable persons in the municipality.

speechtext: In this part of the act the municipality comes into the situation only if it decides to assume itself the position of a lending institution. That is, the local authority becomes the lender, and as the lender it enters into an agreement with the minister in the same manner as any private lending institution would do. Then of course the local authority becomes just the same as any other lender having to put in a great deal of its own money. No local authority has yet availed itself of that privilege, and I gave some consideration in the redrafting of the bill to the question whether it would be desirable to leave in connection with part I the right to a municipality to become itself the lending institution. I thought, having regard to all the possibilities which might arise, that it was desirable to leave it in such a position. It has never occurred yet, but I can conceive of its occurring in places where the municipality exists for one industry, and the industry might desire that the municipality should become for that municipality only a lender under the terms of part I. We do not bar that, but of course if a municipality does become a lender under the terms of part I, it must comply with all the provisions which the minister must exact from private lending institutions.

Two years ago I secured a loan under the Dominion Housing Act through the Sun Life Assurance Company, and built a house. This I consider very unfair. If I should meet with an accident or be sick, or for any other reason fail to make one monthly payment then I lose all the money I have put into the property, which in this case amounts to $4,300, the loan being $5,700. I took this matter up with the Deputy Minister of Finance at the time. He agreed that it was unfair but did not see what he could do about it.
In a case of this kind, where a man in fairly good circumstances has an equity of almost fifty per cent in the building, and through some misfortune is unable to make his payments for two or three months, if the owner of another part of the equity then forecloses it is most unfair that the borrower should not have ample opportunity of redeeming his property. speechtext: If the hon. member will look into it, I think he will see that this provision is not applicable in any province other than Quebec. The old principle, "once a mortgage always a mortgage" is the foundation of our whole system of jurisprudence with respect to the foreclosure of the equity of redemption. But that does not apply to the province of Quebec. In our western country we used to provide that the mortgagor should, in the event of default, attorn to the mortgagee and become a tenant at a rental equivalent to the payment which was to be made. That still obtains, I think, in some provinces, although I believe some had it taken out. The one rule that the supreme court in two or three cases, notably that of Williams v. Box, which came from Manitoba, laid down, was "once a mortgage always a mortgage," and no contractual agreement or terms of any understanding between the parties could foreclose that equity of redemption on the question of its being subject to redemption on the part of the mortgagor at any time while the mortgagee held title to it. But in the province of Quebec the situation is entirely different. I believe the hon. member will find on investigation that, while that reads as a very drastic provision, in practice it will be impossible for the company to secure title to the property without taking appropriate proceedings to that end, and the mere declaration in the contract that failure to make or default in making the payments called for has the effect of vesting the property in the mortgagee is not to be taken as severely as it reads.

This is a very important section of the bill and one which I hope will be made use of to a very large extent. I know that there are very many people who are anxious to take advantage of this provision to build small homes valued at between $2,500 and $3,000. At the present time there is a shortage throughout the country of that type of home for small families. One thing I was afraid of a year or two ago when we passed the housing act. During the course of the discussion then I spoke of the fear I had that the men engaged in selling the commodities necessary for the building of houses would increase their prices when there was a demand for their materials, and I believe it was so. After the passing of the act, when construction became a little brisker than usual, the cost of material went up in many instances, and I am afraid that unless there is some kind of check kept by those responsible for the administration of the present bill when it goes into effect we may again have an increase in the prices of the various commodities that go into the construction of houses. In that event the equity which a person may have of ten or fifteen per cent would be wiped out automatically by the increased cost of materials.
I wonder if the minister has in mind any means of preventing such an increase in the cost of commodities. We want to encourage people to put up decent homes at the prices contemplated in this particular section of the bill. I know the task is a very difficult one and it means that the minister may have to regulate, to some extent perhaps unofficially, the cost of building material. But in the

speechtext: My hon. friend knows how difficult that question is. Section 3 of this bill gives the minister power to make an investigation with respect to factors entering into the cost of construction and as to the feasibility of securing economies and increased efficiency. That provision is there to enable the minister to have machinery whereby he can investigate causes which might operate in increasing costs of material. My hon. friend must recognize of course, as we all do, that there are legitimate reasons for some increases in the prices of commodities, and there are, of course, price increases which we might regard as illegitimate. The minister is given authority under that section to find what the facts are in connection with such a situation, and then, of course, he will have available the machinery of law as it now exists, dependent upon what the cause was found to be. That is as far as I can go in answer to my hon. friend. I have spoken very plainly, both publicly in this house and privately to the construction industry, pointing out that there is one way for this whole program to be killed or to be deprived of its effectiveness, and that is for those engaged in it, no matter who they may be, capital or labour, to regard it as an opportunity for increasing the prices of the commodities they have to sell, irrespective of what those commodities may be. (iv) determine the manner in which losses incurred in connection with loans made under this part shall be established;
I am not going to do more than to say this, and then I shall have concluded all I have to say, and shall be satisfied. This, with other legislation dealing with this subject matter, goes further than most legislation has gone in this country in conferring upon the governor in council-and you will note that I am saying nothing about the Prime Minister's fear of the governor in council in other days- power, authority and jurisdiction to an extent that is not usual. I have suggested that whenever the exercise of that power is legislative in character, it should be published in order that "he that runs may read," so that "wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein." That is the position. If the minister, with his knowledge of legislation, thinks subsection 2 is ample for that purpose, I have done my part in directing attention to the point. I feel that subsection 2 is not ample, in some respects, and I feel it my duty to direct attention to the fact that it is a negation of the theory propounded by the present government as to the powers to be exercised by the governor in council. I am glad that the minister at least has kept before him the distinction between what he conceives to be the exercise of legislative power and the exercise of administrative power. The book to which reference has been made so often, by the lord chief justice of England, was directed against the exercise of legislative power by the executive. It was not directed against the administrative power; for everyone knows that you cannot have laws

National Housing Act
if you undertake to set out in a statute all the details of administration. You must clothe with power the officials charged with responsibility, and the governor in council must name the persons to discharge that responsibility. But when you get into the legislative field you are dealing with another matter altogether, because this parliament is asked to confer upon a committee of parliament, namely the cabinet, power to legislate, which of course is the negation of Magna Charta itself, as one of my hon, friends from Toronto would say. It is the negation of it; but at the same time, if the minister thinks this is ample for his purpose, I have served mine by making the distinction abundantly clear.
When an executive exercises legislative power pursuant to authority given by parliament, this has been regarded as the beginning of autocracy, and it was the anathemas thundered against the late government by the present Prime Minister with respect to matters less important from a legislative standpoint that brought about so much discussion in this chamber. The Smiling face of the Minister of National Defence is always there to remind me of the fact that at all times, in dealing with these matters, he would be ready to join in that well known psalm "I the sinner am," or probably, with respect to a matter of this kind, "I the chief sinner am."

I should like to direct the attention of the minister to one feature which I think should be considered. I found that a great many people who desired to take advantage of the act as it existed previously found great difficulty in ascertaining what they had to do, the nature of the thing and so on. In fact, many told me that they had endeavoured to find out from institutions such as insurance companies and so forth, which were more or less agents for the handling or administration of the act, and that those institutions were so vague in their knowledge of the matter that these people had just given up hope of getting any accurate information. This clause has to do with the terms, conditions and so on that will govern, and what the applicants must do or must know in order to determine whether they desire a loan or can comply with the terms.
I think there is a danger, and I should like to point out one or two clauses and then indicate where that danger may be. Paragraph (ii) of subsection 1 provides for the prescribing of sound standards of construction. In the United States they have a bureau of standards, which publishes certain standards regarding cement, electrical equipment and the 
various branches of construction. These standards are established, fixed and definite, and are accepted and conformed to by the building industry. We have no such standards here.

speechtext: Yes; but we have no such standards established here, although the national research council did have the matter in hand, I know, and did hope to establish such standards. I know there are certain standards set up within the industry itself, and the national research council had some part in that, but here we must have uniform standards for all, because you may prescribe standards in one part of the country and, if the governor in council chose to change that order in council a month later, you might have another standard. That is where the fine distinction comes in between legislation and administration. I think we should surround this legislation with the utmost safeguard, so there will be the least possible tendency to change it, and so that it may be made as perfect as possible before it is promulgated.

Will my hon. friend let me deal with that point before he goes on to the next one? He has put his finger upon one great difficulty I found in attempting to administer the old housing act, particularly with respect to providing standard specifications. They were too difficult. First, there could not be a standard specification for the whole of Canada; that became obvious very early in the work we were doing. Second, there was that absence of real standards to which the hon. member refers. Towards the end of last year I directed the attention of the national research council to this problem, and as a result the national research council,
I think, in January, summoned a meeting of all the elements which might be conceivably be concerned with it. I was present at the meeting, and the ground work was there laid for studies which would lead to accepted standards along basic lines such as those which my hon. friend has suggested. Of course it will not be a quick matter, and the grave problem of diverse climatic and other conditions in various parts of Canada does not make it easier; but I agree that we must attain something of the results which have been attained-although they are not by any means universally acclaimed in the United States-by the bureau of standards of that country in relation to the building industry there. For the present, however, we had to evolve specifications under the Dominion Housing Act; we had to do the best we

National Housing Act
could with the material at hand; we had to make the best decisions we could, in consultation with the construction industry, architects and others, for the various parts of Canada. And that has been done in our standard specifications as they now exist. I may tell my hon. friend what I believe he will be rather pleased to hear, namely, that in the correspondence I receive the attacks made on the specifications are always that they are too stiff; that a little lighter construction here and cheaper there would do as well. It is the usual contest between the technical men and the practical men as to what can be done. I try to avoid getting on either side, but to find the best from both, and we are making progress in that regard as a result of contacts which the housing division maintains with the construction industry.
With respect to people knowing about the law, it early became apparent from our experience with the act that generally speaking, people in those areas in which lending institutions were not prepared to lend, would not know much about it. It was for that reason that we evolved in pamphlet form publicity material descriptive of the whole scheme, of which pamphlets many thousands of copies have been distributed; they are going out all the time in response to requests which my hon. friend will appreciate come constantly to the department. But that has not overcome the difficulty of lending in the more remote districts. That we hope to overcome by other provisions.

speechtext: What brought the minister to the idea of an income five times the rental? Is the rental of the average workman in Canada not about fourteen per cent rather than twenty per cent? Did the minister fix the price arbitrarily?

subtopic: MEASURE TO ASSIST THE CONSTRUCTION OF HOUSES-PROVISIONS WITH RESPECT TO LOW RENTAL HOUSES AND MUNICIPAL TAXES
speechtext: It was a question of finding a fair means of measurement, and after taking into account all the bases of economic rent elsewhere, the experience which has developed elsewhere in regard to the schemes, and 3uch information as is available to us in that regard from our own bureau of statistics, we reached the conclusion that five times is about right. If the municipality is the authority set up, the province must help by way of its guarantee and the municipality must help by way of maximum tax provision. What we have in mind as developing under this scheme principally is large-scale projects of flats. We hope that in the area surrounding Montreal something of that sort will occur through the operation of the limited-dividend corporation. In one or two other places it may very well develop by action of the municipality. Would the minister consider the possibility of the purpose of this bill being facilitated by the persuasive measures with industrial concerns? No matter what inducements are offered, there are many communities that feel they are being discriminated against, and yet it would not be sound business for any financial institution to engage in operations in such places. It seems to me, however, that where there are substantial industries which are not in the red-they must have reserves if their businesses are to be carried on on a proper basis-they might be persuaded to undertake construction of houses for their employees, which would do away with a lot of red tape and obligations and responsibilities. In such a case the firm would build a house and deduct from the employee's pay cheque each month such a sum of money as might be agreed upon so that he could carry on for the rest of the month.
Perhaps I might be forgiven for citing the operations that are going on at Trail. That company's first thought is the convenience of the employees, because they are convinced
National Housing Act

that this is the first step towards efficiency, and for that purpose they have let a contract for the construction of 240 houses. They have selected a desirable location midway between Trail and Rossland, and these 240 houses are now under construction. Each will have concrete basement, a furnace, four rooms and a modem bathroom on the first floor, and the second floor will be so arranged that it can be finished by the employee himself at his own convenience. The construction of these houses is substantial, and the cost is at the very minimum, far lower than the employee himself could build a house by his own contract. These houses are for the use of employees only and are sold only to employees. The employee can pick out his location and purchase his house at the minimum cost. The cost will range between $2,200 and $2,300. An employee is permitted in the first place to rent at such a figure as covers the rent and five per cent interest and amortization; at the end of the year, if he thinks he would like to own the house, the rent he has paid for that year will apply on the purchase, and he will carry on his payments, which are deducted from his cheque each month. There are few complications and very little of the intricacy inevitable in small communities.
As regards advertising in the Gazette, in my opinion anyone who wants to hide information instead of giving it to the public should choose the Gazette. I had occasion to inquire as to the circulation of the Gazette last year, and I was informed that they were distributing 1,053 copies throughout the dominion. Many of these copies go to members and very few to lawyers. I should like to know, therefore, what particular use there is in advertising in the Gazette.

prevent a corporation, such as the type of

corporation to which my hon. friend has referred, from operating under part I of this act, as in fact some of them have operated under the old housing act. I believe it is generally known-I am not giving away anybody's secret-that in the town of Comeau Bay there was a housing development so arranged by one of the lending institutions, and guaranteed by the industrial corporation developing the property. A similar development is possible elsewhere. In the case most familiar to my hon. friend, the industrial concern has preferred to develop its own housing scheme, under its own control, instead of having anything to do with a lending institution. But it is competent for any such corporation to make arrangements with lending institutions under part I.
With respect to part II, which deals with low-rental housing, there would be nothing to prevent any industrial corporation from becoming itself a limited dividend corporation under the terms of that part for the purpose of supplying low rental houses to its own employees, provided it is prepared to accept the responsibilities imposed upon it by that part. While part II does impose provincial government responsibility where the authority is municipal, no provincial government responsibility is involved where the housing authority is a limited dividend corporation, so that it is possible, even in provinces where the provincial government cannot see their way clear to comply with the conditions with respect to municipalities undertaking low rental housing schemes under part II, that in such provinces there may be, as I am reasonably sure there will be, instances where the limited dividend corporation method can be followed.

In view of the possibility of municipalities becoming local housing authorities, I was glad indeed to hear the minister and the hon. member for Kootenay West enlarge upon the possibility of corporations undertaking building schemes for their own employees. The experience of the Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company in connection with workers' houses in Trail, British Columbia, is beyond the experimental stage, and has proven a boon to their employees. The experience of the Imperial Oil Company and other corporations in Regina along similar lines has proven most beneficial to employees and I suggest might well be undertaken by other industrial corporations in various parts of Canada.
A difficulty I foresee in a municipality becoming a local housing authority is found in a provision in the law of the western provinces, and one which, I believe, is found in the law of Ontario, that a municipality borrowing money for any municipal purpose whatsoever can do so only by by-law submitted to the burgesses, and carried by a two-thirds majority. That means that the class which it is intended this measure shall benefit would be excluded from voting on the by-law. Only a property owner would have a right to express himself.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, May 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Woods-worth for the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the criminal code.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe this bill is of sufficient importance to deserve a more extended discussion than possibly the temper of the house at this moment will permit. No one who has taken part in this debate has as yet expressed any disagreement with the principle involved. Certainly the slightest knowledge of the character of the present economy of the world must suggest that workers should have the right to organize in the same measure as employers. Keeping in mind the experience of older countries, particularly the United Kingdom where the labour movement grew up at first under a cloud of suppression and later under the shadow of respectability, one would hope to have the progress of trade unions generally in this country proceed along similar lines.
Before expressing my view on the merits of the bill and in order that I may not appear to be giving expression to something merely for the purposes of the moment, I should like to quote from a speech I made in a radio series along with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) and others dealing with this general problem. I do this in order that the hon. gentleman who is sponsoring this bill may not suggest that I am supporting the principle of the bill to-night after having taken a contrary stand at an earlier date. I stated my views long before this bill was introduced in this chamber. I am quoting my own words not because
(Mr. Dunning.]
they are of special significance, but because they indicate clearly my own views before the bill was introduced. I said:
It is not enough for a man to be able to think freely. This would be indeed a one-sided liberty, which would not be freedom at all. A man must be free to associate with his fellowmen for joint action in realms where there is a community of interest. The difficulty arises, not so much with the denial of this right of association, as with the measure of control which the state is entitled to use over voluntary associations; and this raises one of the most, difficult problems of political science.
And further:
Liberty must reside within the context of this restrictive basis, but this restriction itself must be defined.
I ask the hon. member who is sponsoring this bill to follow particularly what I am going to read. Perhaps very few members will subscribe to it, but it represents my view and indicates how I thought then and still think about these matters. I quote:
A government is not justified in suppressing an association, the mere beliefs of which are subversive of the existing order. The occasion for governmental interference must be when the association has moved to action unmistakably in an attempt to bring about an overthrow of the estalished order.
I can go the whole way with the hon. gentleman in the expression of a belief in the principle of freedom of association as applied to workers and to all other groups within the state. I think it would be unfortunate if the hon. member were to suggest that because of the observations of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), the government had expressed a view contrary to the principle of this bill. The Minister of Labour indicated clearly that he believed in the principle of the bill. He did not object to it except on one ground that must be obvious to all. He said that the law officers of the crown having determined that this was not within the constitutional powers of this government, it would be a matter almost of political immorality if we passed something so clearly outside our authority. The Minister of Labour made a statement a year ago, to which he referred in his remarks during this debate. I think that statement bears repetition to-night. The Minister of Labour was speaking on behalf of the government, and his statement indicates the temper of the administration with respect to this whole matter. He said:
It is necessary to state in the clearest terms that the right of association is a civil right, long established by law and usage. It was affirmed with special reference to Canada by an order in council of July 11, 1918 (P.C. 1743). It

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
was proclaimed explicitly in the Treaty of Versailles at the close of the world war. To deny the right of workmen to combine in any lawful organization they desire for the promotion of their common welfare is an open invitation to extremists to preach the futility of collective bargaining as an alternative to direct action. The right of association for legitimate purposes should be respected in the national interest and labour should not be denied the means of organizing for collective bargaining. The right of employers to organize for all lawful purposes is not questioned in any quarter. Employers are not entitled in the same breath to protest against governmental regulation of industry and to deny to labour its right to resort to legitimate measures of self-help through voluntary association.
That is a very strong declaration. I think it was the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr Stevens) who stated that the order in council passed shortly after the war was merely a pious declaration. I suppose the same thing could be said with regard to this statement. The reason they may have merely the effect of pious declarations is that the matter concerned does not come within the constitutional powers of this parliament.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
At the moment this
assumption of authority is being exercised by the provinces. In Nova Scotia we have the Nova Scotia Trade Unions Act, 1937. In British Columbia we have the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act. In Manitoba we have the Strikes and Lock-outs Prevention Act, 1937. In Quebec we have the Fair Wages Act, and we have acts that were recently passed in Saskatchewan and New
Brunswick. I quite agree that in some respects these acts lack the necessary teeth to deal with the problem. I would say that, certainly with regard to at least three provincial acts, but that does not, one way or the other, affect the problem.
I submit, and I put this to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr Woods-worth), that the law officers of the crown having decided that this matter comes under the caption of property and civil rights it would not be justifiable for this or any other government or any parliament to act contrary to that advice There may be methods of determining whether or not that advice is correct, but in so far as the measure now stands before the house there is, I submit, no other course open to us.
In addition, I would suggest this, that in respect of the servants of the dominion or in respect of labour in those parts of Canada not coming within the organized provinces we have the power to enact legislation covering them, and having in mind that legislative competence I would, speaking for myself, agree to the application of this bill to them. I do not want the hon. gentleman to misconstrue what I have been saying, and I am sure he will not. While to some this bill may seem extravagant in its extent, it is nevertheless a bill which in our day deserves support in principle. I believe that if it were constitutionally possible it should be made a crime, as my hon. friend suggests, in the case of an attempt to prevent the proper organization by labour to obtain its legitimate rights. Representing as I do a constituency where labour is to be found in great numbers, I appreciate that point more perhaps than anyone else. I was going to make a personal reference, but I leave that out.
I suggest to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that even if we had the power of passing this bill-and assuming the power I would agree that we should pass it

that is not in the long run going to be the effective way of protecting the rights of workers through organizations and the like. The Minister of Justice referred to the tradition in England. I wish we had the same tradition in this country, and then the events that took place in this province in the course of the last-year would not have been possible. I agree with all that. I agree that it was wise for the hon. gentleman to bring forward this method of trying to have this house assert in no uncertain manner its views, and because oi that I am taking part in this discussion, but I suggest to him. as one who knows the
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

tradition in the common law countries, as one who knows conditions in respect of the handling of this matter in other places, that the effective way has never been the use of coercion, and that method will never be a guarantee in itself.
Reference was made in this house in the admirable statement by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) to the position in Sweden. Of course, there you have altogether a different problem, just as in the United States you have under the Wagner Act an altogether different situation, in so far as the question of jurisdiction is concerned.
If any hon. member suggests, and I think it has been suggested in this debate, that the Minister of Justice takes his stand because he happens to come from a province where there seem to be restrictions which, speaking for myself, I certainly do not countenance, I submit that the Minister of Justice long before this measure was introduced into this house did give expression to the proper method of bringing about the realization of the rights of labour. That expression of his could be given in England because it is so often thought that French-Canadians themselves do not appreciate the full import of the words "liberty" .and "freedom" and all that they mean. Let me quote from a speech made by the Minister of Justice, speaking at a communist [DOT]gathering in Montreal, where he was opposed to the use of force as a means of coercing the communists, and what he said there might equally in reverse order be applied to this whole problem. He said:
(Translation) If we would secure for ourselves political as well as economic security, if we wish to repulse successfully the onsets of the enemies of order, we must depend less ou the criminal code, on the police force and the gaols, and more on personal dignity, on individual efforts and on cooperation, which make up the substance and the soul of a free people. Guns and hand grenades are of no avail against those who preach violence, be the reasons good or bad. With an enlightened mind, we must accept necessary changes and unavoidable reforms, if we would take from the enemies of order the weapons provided them because of certain errors and abuses.

question, if I may, to the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). It seems that his objection was that we did not have the power in this parliament to deal with the matter. speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I confess I
was not able to follow the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in the observations he made a few days ago based upon the report made by his officials that this proposed act now in the form of a bill is ultra vires of this parliament in its entirety.
I followed the speech made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) this evening, and I could not help thinking of one of his illustrations. He said that he had a few weeks ago declared that man's belief was one thing but that unless he expressed it in oveyt acts he saw no reason to complain. He reversed the process in the speech we listened to this evening, and while his apology for the administration was admirable, the only way in which I think there can be an expression of an overt act would be by voting for the measure; for there can be added to it without any difficulty a provision that it shall not come into force until proclaimed, and in the meantime it could be referred to the courts to determine its validity.
I think the right hon. Minister of Justice will agree with me that in two paragraphs of this bill we are not dealing with property and civil rights at all, that what we are dealing

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
with is intimidation and conspiracy. In the paragraph to which I refer, paragraph (b), we are dealing with the offence of intimidation. We are dealing with an offence against the body politic on the part of those who may be in a position to enforce their views by threats, intimidation or otherwise, preventing that which arises out of property and civil rights, namely a contract being made effective. No one would question the right of the provinces to control matters of property and civil rights. No one has questioned the right of the provinces to deal with matters of contract. But it does not follow that because that is so, this parliament in the exercise of its jurisdiction over criminal law may not express itself in the Strongest possible terms as to those who interfere with freedom of contract and the making of it. It is with respect to this that my difficulty arises.
This legislation in the last two paragraphs deals only with matters in which by force, by intimidation, by threats-the character of the threats and the extent of the intimidation are not the issue-an effort is made on the part of one person to prevent another person from exercising a civil right. The civil right is, as indicated by the last speaker, the right to belong to a union or to an association, the right to do as a man pleases with respect to the matter of collective bargaining. If the other person said, "You shall not exercise that civil right," and stops there, well and good; but if by intimidation, by threats, by the power and authority and force of his position he says " 'Thou shalt not' exercise your civil rights," that is a matter of criminal law; that establishes our right to exercise our jurisdiction with respect to it, which wo are doing every day. All one needs to do is to read the criminal code and note its provisions with respect to mischief and matters of that kind, with which I shall not trouble the house to-night. That does not conflict at all with the right of the provinces to deal as they please with matters of contract, of property, of civil rights. But where a man says, " ' Thou shalt not' use your property or exercise your civil rights," and he uses towards you intimidation or force or threats to see that you do not exercise your rights, that is an offence; that is within the criminal law, and solely within the jurisdiction of this parliament. It is that offence at which this bill strikes.
I am now dealing with the two paragraphs at the end of the bill. Look at the next paragraph. Is it or is it not a criminal offence if a man "conspires, combines, agrees or arranges with any other employer or his agent"
to do any of these things? Is it wrong, as a matter of law, to conspire to do an illegal act? Well, the criminal law is clear on that point. There may be a conspiracy which is a combination to do a lawful thing. Against that the law does not strike. But when there is an agreement between parties to do an unlawful thing the criminal law interposes. And what have you here? You have here intimidation, threats to deprive a person of what the hon. member for Essex East so well described as the exercise of a civil right -freedom of association, freedom of speech. I was reading a book the other day, The Voice of England with respect to Freedom. Starting away back a thousand years ago, and along down through all the centuries, the voice of England has been the voice of freedom. Here we have a combination or association which is permitted by law, and we see, in the last paragraph to which I am directing attention, that if you combine and agree to do an unlawful act, namely prevent a man from belonging to an association or trade union, you are liable to the criminal law of the country. Have we not jurisdiction there ?
There remains one other matter, and that is the first paragraph. You can read that in a sense which is consonant with the views expressed by the minister, but I do not so read it. The first paragraph deals with refusal to employ or the dismissal from employment of any person for the reason that he has exercised his freedom of choice by belonging to a union which is formed for the purpose of advancing in a lawful manner the interest of the workmen. If it is a penalty for a breach of contract, then of course I have no difficulty in agreeing with the minister. But it is not a penalty for a breach of contract, because that is covered by a provincial statute; that penalty sounds in damages, as many acts provide. This bill goes further. It does not, as I read it, contemplate the question of contract or property and civil rights in that sense at all. It merely says that if a man refuses to employ another, or dismisses him from his employment because he has exercised his freedom of choice by associating himself with a particular trade union, that is such a deprivation of a civil right, the great right of freedom or association, as to incur the penalties of the criminal law, and not a pecuniary result, sounding in damages. That, I think, is the distinction between the provincial statutes and this bill. Of course I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Essex East, reflecting in that respect the mind and almost the speech of the Minister of Justice. We should not
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

openly pass laws which, in the opinion of those responsible for their promulgation, are ineffective and invalid. On the other hand, if we have what I conceive to be the strongest reason in the world for believing a statute to be valid, we should place it on the statute books and ask that it be referred to the court so that its validity may be determined. That is the method prescribed by law for that purpose. I am sure the minister will remember the very strong words used by the late Edward Blake as to the desirability of that course being followed in dealing with a matter of this kind.
I believe the bill to be valid. I believe it to be within the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament. I believe it makes it an adequate and proper offence for a person to interfere with any man exercising his freedom of choice and his right of association, provided always that it is exercised-in the language of the bill itself-" in a lawful manner." By those words we should, I feel, all be bound-"in a lawful manner," consonant with the laws of the country, with its institutions, with everything they imply. I support the bill.

speechtext:
I rise to endeavour, if I can, to correct an impression which I believe was left during the time that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) spoke, and again to-night when the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) spoke in connection with the measure at present before the house. I judge from the remarks of the two hon. gentlemen who spoke on this matter, and particularly from what was said by the Minister of Labour, referring to the old country in comparison with Canada, that Great Britain is one country to be followed because in regard to labour legislation they have not placed a great deal of it on the statute books. The Minister of Labour suggested that we in Canada would perhaps do well if we followed the same line as Great Britain. Well, as one who in early youth came from there, and had belonged and still belongs to a trade union, I can tell the Minister of Labour this: The reason there is little on the statute books of Great Britain with regard to labour or trade union legislation is that for many long years labour and the working people had no representation in the British House of Commons. In the early days of the fight for trades unions, members of the House of Commons comprised in large measure land owners, steel mill owners and coal mine owners. The history of the trade union movement in Great Britain is one which I think should be told to the world. The fight put up in the early days by the working
(Mr. Bennett.]
people of the old land for trade union legislation was a very tragic one indeed; it was one of bloodshed, starvation, intimidation, trial, and in many instances, flight from their homes to other lands. I believe that other countries have benefited to some extent in consequence of what the workers did.
I am all for the principle of this bill, and I intend to vote for it, though it may not be within the purview of the dominion government ; and I do so not only because I represent a considerable section of labour in the constituency of New Westminster, but also because I have vivid recollections of the early days of that struggle for trade unionism when this very principle was being advocated in the old land. We in this country have a good deal of reason to be grateful for the fight that was made in those early days in Great Britain, and I should like to see this legislation put into effect in every province in Canada. We are, or should be, heading in that direction. We may not reach the goal immediately, but -we shall utimately come to the point where all the provinces will give absolute freedom to labour to organize.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this bill, and I have no notes-perhaps you will say, "Thank goodness"-so I shall have to think on my feet. This is not a government bill; but I know something of the tasks of the toiler; I know something of his struggle. When I came out of university in my first year the only job I could get was wheeling bricks at fifteen cents an hour, and the third day after I had been at that job my hands were in such a state that I could not hold on to a baseball as well as I did *to-night. I know something of the struggles of the labourers in Winnipeg in those early days. They comprised English, Scotch, Irish, Icelandic and Swedish, and I was one of them. I cast my lot in with them. I can say that they were as fine a group of men as ever struck this great Canada of ours and there are hundreds of them to-day who are not wheeling bricks. Of course, I admit that I did not have to stay at that very long because the contractor, who was going into big business just then, thought I might assist him in his office work and take charge of the labourers.
When I hear that some members of this house hold their breath when a preacher comes around, I can tell them that I have heard language which would put them to shame, because I have heard men who could swear even scientifically. I was an officer of the first labour union in the city of Winnipeg, and we wondered why it was that we should

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
have to work for fifteen cents an hour when bricklayers were getting forty-five cents. Some of us were green, of course, but none of us were yellow. As I think of those men and the struggle they had to make for their rights, I can recall how they used to sober up a little and keep their cheques in order that they might be able to pay their board and keep their wives and families in difficult times. In those days I formed habits and trains of thought which I have not changed. I take second place to no man in this house in my interest in the toiler, and I will take no part in anything that will cast reflection on the honest toiler. I may tell the house parenthetically that if we had more employers of labour like an hon. minister who comes from some place near Fort William, it would be better for the country, because when the depression came he did not say to his office hands and his workers, "I have no more contracts; take a rest for a while". W'hat he did tell his office hands and his workers was this, "Employ yourselves as best you can; your cheques will come just the same". No wonder I stand behind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe). When he did not have to, he treated the honest toiler in a generous way. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I know something of the struggles of the working man, and I know why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has brought in this bill. Some of our employers of labour do not know how to treat the honest toiler; they do not give him fair play: I have known employers who would organize themselves into an association and then refuse to let their workers organize.
I belong to a party in this house as progressive as any in the dominion, and when we get a free fling, as, thank goodness, we get it in caucus, though I must not tell tales out of school, I can tell you it is the finest thing I have ever struck. We are not muzzled, and you will never hear the crack of the whip, as some people think. But, like other hon. members, I feel that I am free to vote just as I please, and I am going to vote for this bill if somebody does not talk it out. Having said that, therefore, I shall now sit down, thanking you, Mr. Speaker, and the house.
