Coming from the province of Quebec, where our first magistrate is so scrupulous about provincial autonomy. I think it right to do my share in seeing that this House of Commons does not override his very important point with regard to rights in that province. As everyone knows. Hon. Mr. Duplessis in some circumstances is protesting against some
federal legislation, because he is convinced that we are overriding the autonomy of the province of Quebec. And in some other cases he claimed otherwise. I shall not enter into the question of the constitutionality of this bill because that was covered pretty well by previous speakers, the distinguished Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), and on the other side, the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) who is sponsoring the bill. But as far as I can compare this legislation with some legislation which has been overruled and found ultra vires, I do not see any difference at all. We must admit that we are in such a situation to-day that we have to accept the constitution passed in 1867, and we have to deal with it according to the interpretation given by the highest court of this country, the privy council. If that is true, what is the use of this house spending time, and what is more important, spending money, to pass legislation which after great expense for fees may be declared ultra vires of this parliament. And, mind you, I am a lawyer; I am speaking against my own interest; it might be that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would be inclined to choose me as his attorney in that case. But I try to take a higher view than my personal interests, and consider the interest of this country first. I believe it is our duty as legislators to prevent this bill from becoming law, because we know beforehand that the result would be its submission to the supreme court and then to the privy council. And I for one do not want that.
If we compare this bill with legislation which has been enacted in the province of Quebec lately, Bills Nos. 19 and 20, I think the present administration of Quebec have dealt with this matter and the purpose aimed at by this bill now before us. I am firmly convinced that the legislation which has been passed by the Quebec legislature is entirely wrong, if I compare it with the alleged request of the labour men in that province. Nevertheless I believe the premier of Quebec is right in claiming that in the situation in which we find ourselves to-day, due to the British North America Act, the right to legislate in such matters belongs to the province. I am sure the premier of Quebec is wrong when he refuses to consent to this parliament dealing with this social legislation. I am convinced that so long as some provinces refuse to this parliament the right to legislate in social matters, the result will be against the interest of our provinces. I know perfectly well, and hon. members will agree, that if we
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

are left in that unfavourable situation as regards social legislation-take, for instance, the question of unemployment insurance, if one province decides to pass a law to establish unemployment insurance and other provinces refuse to do it-the consequence is clear. The people engaged in such industries which fall under that law will move from the province which refuses to pass the law into some province which has passed the law. On the other hand capitalists who have invested money in such industries will leave the province which has passed the law and go to a province which has refused to pass the law. It is easy to see that so long as the provinces refuse to agree to transfer their right and allow the federal parliament in common understanding for the best interests of the citizens of this country to enact this social legislation, no good result will be attained.
So far as the principle of Bill No. 4 is concerned, I might be ready to agree with it. Of those in this house who are in favour of justice, who want to see the citizens of this free country have their share of sunshine, who are against oppression, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville is one. But the duty to see that there is a sure right for employees to enjoy free association, and that employers should not do anything to molest or prevent their employees from associating for their common good, is the duty of the province. What is the use of our passing such legislation as this when we know perfectly well it is ultra vires? As to this, however, I am ready to respect the views of those who differ with me, who have at their head the right hon. leader of the opposition. Nine o'clock. SUPPLY
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Marketing services-Live stock and poultry- further amount required, $7,040.

The hon. member for
Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) had quite a lot to say when this item was last before the committee. I cannot vouch for the accuracy of his statements, but because of his experience as a member of this house and as a minister having charge of the very department to which he referred, I think his words should receive some attention from the committee. He stated that some of the packing institutions have been making monkeys out of the officers of the department. I have sometimes thought the members of parliament have been treated in almost the same way. Since I entered this house I have come to the conclusion that members have not a great deal to say about the legislation and regulations that are passed. Those matters are mostly settled in the departments. This is irksome to me. I have always prided myself on being able to take my own part. When I was elected to this house I figured I could do more than my share in the house. I considered what I was fitted for, and I decided that perhaps I could so something for the live stock industry of this country.
Let me say that I have received nothing but the utmost courtesy from the officials of the Department of Agriculture. Any time I wanted information I always got it if it was within their power to give it to me. I believe enough evidence has been presented in the last few years to warrant the minister in asking for an investigation into the live stock industry. My conclusion is that we should have a better system than we have at the present time. I am not suggesting the appointment of a roving, meandering royal commission, but I contend that at the very first of the session next year-it is too late to do anything this year-a select committee should be appointed to deal with this matter. In the meantime hon. members can obtain all the information possible in order that they will be able to deal intelligently and expeditiously with this question. We have had too many royal commissions. Nine times out of ten, when a royal commission is appointed, it is appointed to evade responsibility. I come from a farming district and farming is the only business with which I am conversant.
I feel I should have some responsibility in investigating a question of this kind. I could make a number of suggestions, but I shall be satisfied with making just one. We might very well consider the selling of live stock by means of auctions as they do in the old country. I believe that is worth considering as a new method of marketing our cattle in the stock-yards.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
I quite appreciate what the hon.
member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has had to say with regard to the necessity of an inquiry being made into the methods of handling live stock in Canada. However,
I may say that it is the intention of the department as at present organized to carry on that kind of investigation continuously. I agree with much of what the hon. member has said with regard to meandering investigations being more or less a means of shifting responsibility on certain occasions. It was for that reason that in reorganizing the department we set up a marketing branch which would be continuously in contact with all the activities of the stock-yards and marketing in general. I am hopeful that with the completion of the reorganization we shall be able, in the year that is ahead of us, to carry on an investigation that will be effective at all times throughout the year.
I think we can accomplish more by that method than by the appointment of a committee. However, I have no objection to a committee being appointed. It could be appointed whether or not I objected, because that is the right of the house. If a committee is appointed, the department will be

Supply-Agriculture-Live Stock
ready to cooperate in every way possible. However, I repeat that this work can. be done more effectively by the officials who are continuously in touch with the activities of the stock-yards and the packing plants. I think I can say to the hon. member that such an investigation will be carried on continuously throughout the year.

I do not believe the live stock men of this country will be satisfied with the form of investigation to which the minister has referred. I know there are serious objections to the methods being used at the present time, and there is an increasing demand that some investigation should be made into these matters. The department of agriculture of Manitoba conducted an investigation into these matters this winter. I do not know the results of their findings, but they must have discovered something. We could use that. In the meantime, we could use this United States trade agreement. All this evidence would be available for this committee next year. I am firmly convinced that this is the proper way to carry on the investigation, and there is no doubt that an investigation is needed. I know there are hon. members coming from rural constituencies who are just aching to take a more prominent part in the work of parliament.

For some time I have thought there was something radically wrong with the marketing of live stock. When I was discussing this matter with a farmer he told me that the main trouble to-day is the fact that there are no drovers going up and down the country making competitive bids for live stock. The reason for that is that there is no competition at the big markets such as Toronto and Winnipeg. In the old days the drovers used to run up and down the country and try to buy direct from the farmer, and when the farmer did not get what he thought was the right price he did not have to sell; but to-day he has to send his cattle to Toronto or Winnipeg and sell them on a commission basis, and as was suggested by the hon. member for Kootenay East he has simply to take what is left, which is sometimes extremely little. I have known cases where there was nothing left. Certainly the farmer cannot continue to market his products on that basis and make money.
It is quite true that advice is being given by men who are watching the operations of the big markets and trying to advise the fanner. Over the radio on certain days you will hear these men advising the farmers 
to ship a certain kind of stock to market. I have known farmers who listened to that advice and then went to the best drover they knew and told him to come to their farm and pick up the stock needed for that kind of market, but they found, after they had shipped their cattle, it was the same old story.
When cattle are disposed of, the meat is sold. It is different from selling grain. There is no sample market. The farmer has to take just what he can get for his cattle. I profess I do not know how to cure the situation; I know it would be difficult, because all the small abattoirs have gone out of business. The law of supply and demand is working fairly well at the present time, but we have known times in the last seven or eight years when the farmer got hardly anything for his products, and that is not good for any business. I feel sure that the minister would be well advised to look into the marketing of live stock, and if something can be done I hope it will be done.

Might I suggest to the minister that he refer this matter to the tariff board? I have listened to a great many speeches and read considerable evidence on this matter, and I confess that I have been somewhat bewildered by the views which have been expressed pro and con. It is a matter of vital importance to the farmers of this country. I find, on investigation, there is jurisdiction for the tariff board to deal with this question, and I therefore suggest that the minister ask the tariff board, which is there for the purpose of dealing with matters of this kind, to ascertain the exact facts and make a report which will enable us to understand the situation, if there be any further doubt about it. It is contended that the operations of one firm have brought about certain results. Whether or not that is so is a question of fact. That can be ascertained by the tariff board, which has the powers of inquiry and investigation, and I suggest that if the government would refer the question to the tariff board it might be exceedingly useful. But if we undertake, as the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) suggests, to deal with the matter by a committee of this house, we shall inevitably have certain difficulties which I can foresee. There will always be difficulties in dealing with it by some body other than a body of a judicial nature. The body is there; the jurisdiction is there; the tariff board is there. If the minister would take the appropriate steps to have the facts ascertained by

the board, I think it might be useful alike to himself, to the government, to the great farming body of this country that is so vitally interested, and to the packers themselves.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be pleased to take into consideration the suggestion made by the right hon. leader of the opposition. I should like to have an opportunity of looking into the possibilities of whether that type of inquiry would serve a useful purpose. At the same time I should like to emphasize what I said a moment ago, that with the reorganization of the department as we have it now there will be facilities to make a much more careful inquiry into the whole matter, and not only an inquiry, because I think there is much more required to be done. Regulation and direction are necessary in connection with the whole matter.
There is the view that methods of marketing is partly responsible for some of the criticisms. The system of marketing is passing through a transitional stage on account of the fact that the trucking of live stock has become quite general throughout Canada; indeed, in all countries it is becoming a general practice, and whenever there is such a decided change in the methods of transporting any product as there has been in respect to live stock we are bound to require new regulations and to have new conditions set up for the marketing of that particular product. I think there can be no group of men in Canada better qualified to report on a matter of that kind than the inspectors who have been dealing with it over a long term of years. They must be experts in connection with the business itself; otherwise they are not competent to fill the positions they hold.
But is it not a fact that their long association has created a certain attitude of mind?

I have not found that. The men are new to me. It is only two and a half years since I first became associated with them, and I have found them very fair in their treatment of the whole matter and that they have much the same view as those who are making the complaints. The methods that might be followed are not yet sufficiently apparent because of the newness of the present methods of handling live stock, and those studying the matter have not yet crystallized fully the changes that might be made into regulations to meet the new situation.
To what extent is it different from what has hitherto prevailed?

A man comes in with a truckload of live stock; he goes to the stockyard, looks around and sees what is happening there. He makes up his mind whether the price is satisfactory to him, and, if not, he drives over and sells his stock to the packing plant. It was not so simple when the live stock all came in by trainload and the cars were unloaded at the stock-yards. The packer then had to go to the stock-yards and look for his live stock in any considerable volume. But to-day perhaps more than fifty per cent of the stock are being taken directly to the packing plant without going to the stock-yard at all. New regulations will have to be evolved. The two major factors involved are the commission men in the stock-yards and the large packers operating their own plants.
It is alleged that the packers operate together and have a common price.

On the other hand, it is alleged that the truckers themselves are at the moment one of the most disturbing factors in the whole trade. These things have all to be worked out and methods of marketing adjusted to the new conditions. Again I say I think it requires more than just a board sitting for a few weeks to inquire into the matter. It requires men who have been closely associated with the inspection of the yards and of the packing plants, watching what is going on day by day, and finally working out plans to deal with the situation as it develops.

Dominion area is that area in which the drought was so bad that the federal government decided to assume one hundred per cent responsibility. The provincial area is still in the drought area. People are inclined to designate the area which we were taking care of as the drought area and not consider the other as being in that category, but the provincial area was also part of the drought area. It will be noted that we have no figures for Alberta covering the number of live stock fed.

What is the number
of townships in the dominion area and the number in the provincial area?

The dominion area
covered 170 municipalities in Saskatchewan and fifty-two municipalities in Alberta. The provincial area covered all the remainder of the province in which assistance would be required.
Of any kind?
Of any kind.

Due to drought, the
lack of feed and fodder. It will be noted that there are no figures given for rye and corn in connection with Alberta and for shorts in connection with Saskatchewan.

I think it must be apparent to anyone who has followed this discussion with any degree of care that we have here a problem of considerable magnitude. We have the dominion government exercising jurisdiction over a large area, and we have Saskatchewan-Alberta seems to have had a very small area affected-exercising jurisdiction over what has been called the provincial area. That creates at once a conflict of interest. It must be apparent t-o anyone who has received correspondence that the whole problem of relief in Saskatchewan has been very much complicated by reason of the fact that the dominion government is administering relief on its own responsibility in a given area, and the province is administering it in another area. We did suggest, and I still suggest, that this matter, if it is to be continued, should be dealt with only by a commission.
May I just interject that the administration is carried on by the province over the whole area. The dominion is not administering relief anywhere.
I should have put it in this way. The dominion acquires the food, feed, .fodder and supplies in a given area, and the province does it in another area.
No.
The dominion bought direct.

We bought cheese and
beans and food of that type direct and distributed it to the whole area that was covered by the one hundred per cent federal responsibility.

That is the point I was making. We purchased cheese, dried beans, fish, apples and vegetables. The dominion government went out and purchased these

supplies. We then transported them to Saskatchewan and distributed them, as the minister says, over given areas. On the other hand, we had the province dealing with the situation in the manner indicated by the minister. I submit that in both cases we were dealing with the same taxpayers' money. I submit further-and I do not think this can be questioned-that we have exercised no effective control over the province in connection with this money. That is, while the accounts are audited, there is nothing that prevents the most reckless extravagance on the part of the province because, as the minister very properly says: "The province did this, not the dominion." My contention as to the necessity for a commission was predicated entirely upon that fact.
I have received innumerable letters; but in. view of the fact that it is said that the people have approved this method, I am not going to take the time to argue the matter. It may be said that at the election forty-six per cent of the electors expressed themselves as being in favour of this method. The Saskatoon Phoenix-Star wrote an editorial in which it very properly pointed out that the protest vote in Saskatchewan was larger than the vote the government secured. The editor called it that-"the protest vote"-and he gave the causes for it. It may be said, and is said, "Why waste time talking about this? Saskatchewan has given its verdict; the government is returned, and that is the end of it." We will say that under our democracy that is the end of it, and that we must accept it, except to do one thing. I think the minister will agree with me that when one collecting body, namely, the parliament of Canada, is responsible for the acquisition of the revenue, and another taxing power is spending it, a very difficult situation arises. When we were in office the present Prime Minister spent a very great

Supply-Agriculture-Feed and Fodder
deal of time in reading from learned treatises upon that point, and pointing out how injurious it was to the body politic that it should be continued. We, however, did not discontinue it for reasons that at that moment seemed good. But we did believe that in Saskatchewan, having regard to the very serious character of the situation there, a commission could do the best work possible. The minister disagrees with that. He made that perfectly clear as soon as he came into office because he dispensed with the services of the commission, as he pointed out in this house. Assuming that he is right as to that, I do submit and I wish to put it on Hansard as a matter of record, in the iight of all the complaints, that the matter should be dealt with by a commission.
The minister says that some of the com-olaints are ill-founded. I believe that may be so, but I shall give just one illustration. It is of a blacksmith who was kept so very busy that he was working fifteen hours a day to get his work done; yet he was receiving relief in that community, and he continued to receive relief. The minister very properly says to me: "I have nothing to dio with that, Mr. Bennett, because that matter is dealt with by the province of Saskatchewan, and they assure me that everything is being properly done." But I ask, have we any right to take the money which has been raised by this parliament, and which was referred to yesterday by the minister as being a very large sum indeed, then place it in the hands of other people for expenditure and exercise over it only that control which is involved in being certain that the audit is correct-that the goods are as shown on the invoices, and that there is evidence of delivery of the goods to the amount for which payment is sought? I think not.
I hope, indeed I do more than that, I agree with the very earnest hope expressed by the minister that we shall not have to do this again. But who knows? I do not; for last year when I was west there was promise of a crop, and then a month later there was no promise of a crop. I think there is promise of a better crop this year. I have not been there this spring, but that is what I have been told. We all earnestly hope that there will be a crop. But assume there is not; we have again the responsibility. I urge upon the minister the necessity of considering whether it is not our duty to the people of Canada to set up to deal with this matter some tribunal that will obviate our having to say that this is not in our jurisdiction, and, e converso, for the provinces to say that it is not in theirs. All the money comes from here.
It must be remembered that Saskatchewan has been enabled to carry on its business by reason of the fact that we have provided it with funds. Saskatchewan has not defaulted on its bonds and the insurance companies and investors have received their interest because we have provided the province with the money with which to pay the interest. In Alberta we did not do that, and only one half of the interest on the bonds is covered by the coupons paid. These are facts. I suggest that the time has come when we should consider the possibility of having to face this situation again, and if we have to face it we should realize that we are making a rather heavy call upon the taxpayers of this country, to put up millions of dollars for three purposes:	(1) unemployment relief,
which in Saskatchewan is less, having regard to its agricultural population, than it might otherwise be; (2) relief for drought conditions; and (3) general governmental purposes. Those three make a very large call upon the resources of this dominion. They are subdivided with respect to (2) into very well marked divisions. In one of them we exercise complete and sole control; in the other the provinces exercise complete and sole control.
There should be some body set up-I care not what it may be called-that will be responsible for the administration; for the point to keep in mind is that the government of Saskatchewan is not raising this money by taxation; what it is doing is disposing of the money of Canada which is appropriated by this parliament to them for the purpose- broadly-of relief. Under those circumstances, as the Prime Minister used to point out with great clarity, you cannot expect the same measure of care to be exercised in the disposition of money thus acquired as would be exercised were it to arise from the taxation of the people themselves by the distributing power. I make this suggestion to the minister in the light of what he has pointed out a moment ago, namely that we still have to pay large sums of money. As far as I can see, even if Saskatchewan has a crop we cannot for some time be entirely relieved of responsibility. Is that not correct?
Well, it should not run very far beyond the first of July.
I am very glad to hear the minister say that.
That is, if the crop is in sight.

I must say I am very glad to hear the minister say that, because I
4012	COMMONS
Supply-Agriculture-Feed and Fodder
feared they were so denuded of everything after these many years of drought that until there could be a realization in money, we would have to continue to make contributions to enable them to live, because of lack of purchasing power of any kind, or of credit.
We shall have to continue it to some of them.

These will be matters
largely controlled by the provinces, not by us. I take it that this will be so. The minister will therefore, I think, see the force of what I suggest, namely the desirability of our devising a plan or scheme which will enable us, to exercise more effective control, not necessa rily administrative so far as distribution is; concerned, but with respect to possible abuses in connection with it which are bound to arise where you have any body distributing money or supplies or food or fodder or shelter or clothing, where the responsibility for raising the money is not upon the taxpayers of the province affected. In view of the fact that the electors of Saskatchewan, at least to the extent of forty-six per cent of the population, which under the conditions that prevail constitutes the return of the administration of the day with a minority of the votes, have expressed themselves as being entirely satisfied with the manner in which the distribution of relief has taken place, that must be accepted as an answer-not a bad answer-to any complaint which may be made. But I think it is time that we should carefully and calmly review the situation and, now that the election is past, free from animosities and bitternesses which may have arisen, determine whether or not it is possible to contemplate, with respect to relief, not in Saskatchewan only but in any of the provinces where the federal power is finding the money, that there should be an administration which can effect a closer relationship between the expenditure of money and the results obtained from that expenditure.

There are only one or two remarks I should like to make. I would not like the impression to remain that, in cases such as that recited, of the blacksmith who was very busy and drawing relief all the time, we take no responsibility. Wherever a case of that kind was reported to us, we insisted on an investigation and, where the facts were found to warrant it, a prosecution.

Yes, but we are not
the people to whom reDorts would be made.
[Mr. Bennett.1
Of course we had inspectors out who were checking this work in all parts of the province.

Is it not a fact that
there have been quite a number of prosecutions?

Yes; there have been
quite a number of prosecutions. I do not know whether in this case there has been a prosecution.
There has not been yet.

There have been cases,
and there will be others in which prosecutions are made. But we do take responsibility in that matter.
One other comment I should like to make is that in so far as we have been able to investigate the whole matter of the administrative cost of relief over the whole area, we have found that the closer to the individuals concerned the administration of relief has been handled, the lower the cost has been. The places where we have been able to check indicate that clearly. Take, for example, in Saskatchewan the L.I.D. areas. The municipal department has the same control over the whole area as a municipal council has over a municipality.
That is, the local improvement districts.

Districts that have
not been organized into municipalities, and where the municipal department carries on the activities just as though it were a municipal council. Where the provincial department have been doing that work, at a greater distance from the individuals concerned, the costs have been higher than they have been in the districts where the municipalities have done it.
Ah, but generally speaking these are unsettled districts.

Not in the sense in which the right hon. gentleman speaks. You can find a municipality alongside a local improvement district. They have not been organized 'because they are a little less thickly populated, but one of the chief reasons is that in recent years the people of those areas have found it less costly to operate in that way than to form those areas into municipalities. But when it comes to distributing relief it has been found less costly to have the municipal council do it than even to have an official of the provincial department do it. I think it would be less costly still to have the municipality do it than to have it done by an

official of this government, because of the great distance we are away from the activities in which we are interested.
Oh, yes. Of course we could not do it.

We can judge only from the experiences we have had, and that has been our experience.
Some reference was made to the fact that the 'bond interest has been paid in Saskatchewan largely because of assistance from this government, and that the bond interest in Alberta was not paid because they had not received assistance. I should not like the impression to go out that the reason the bond interest in Alberta was not paid was that they had not received assistance. As a matter of fact, they made a definite decision that they would pay only half the interest whether they received assistance or not. That decision was made without reference to this government, and they have had a great deal of assistance since making that decision. But Saskatchewan never so decided. They said that they would pay the interest if possible, and they have continued to do so.
With regard to the suggestion that the people have voted and that there has been an expression of opinion, which has been a protest expression, I would point out that the protest was much smaller in the area we have been discussing, that is, the area where the dominion government have provided funds and the administration has been carried on by the province, than it was in the other area where there was perhaps less necessity for assistance to be given. I wanted to make that comment because it has a bearing on the question.
What is the percentage cost of distribution?

Yes.
That has been paid by the province, and we have not assisted in that at all. We have, therefore, no accounting of that.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext:
To-day one of our number (Mr. Crerar) has attained another birthday. Full of years and honours he has just come into the

Hon. T. A. Crerar-Birthday Greetings
chamber from reading the messages of congratulation that have come to him from all parts of the world, on the fact that to-day he h3S attained the age of sixty-two. I know he will not regard it as a favour that I should indicate the number of his years; but if he continues to stagger like Atlas under the load he bears, of a department that contains all the mines, resources, parks, forests and Indians, to say nothing of the undetermined question as to whether or not the Eskimos are Indians, it is quite clear that we cannot expect to celebrate more than twenty-five more such anniversaries.
With the hon. gentleman at all times are the best wishes and the good will of all those who have been privileged to be associated with him. He holds very erroneous opinions with great tenacity; and he holds, not with tenacity but with very great ease, the friendship and good will of many people in various parts of this country who are not unmindful of the fact that while oil and water do not mix, it is fitting that the sole representative in this chamber of the union government should, on this, his birthday, sit1 side by side with his right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I wish the hon. minister well.
Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice); I desire to join very heartily with my right hon. friend in expressing congratulations to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar). I am sorry he is getting older. He is getting to be an old man, I understand; in point of fact he is three months older than I am. In regard to the remembrance of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), I think it is true that the Minister of Mines and Resources made a mistake during his lifetime, but I must pay him a tribute.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext:
He has atoned for it.
Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec East); I remember when he was Minister of Agriculture in that union government, facing us poor fellows who were on the other side; I remember having to deliver a speech, which I made as strong as possible, against that nefarious government. The man who was smiling and beaming, facing me at the time I made my speech, was the then Minister of Agriculture; he was lost in his surroundings.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext: Coming events cast their shadows before.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext: So I am pleased indeed to pay him this tribute. He has a fine heart and a sound mind, and he is never very long in his mistakes; he always recovers from them.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext: That is why we have such hope for him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext:
On behalf of the members on this side, I thank the right hon. gentleman for this generous tribute to my colleague.
Mr. CRERAR; Mr. Chairman, I observe that the clock is almost on the stroke of eleven, but certainly I cannot let this occasion pass without expressing to my friend-as I hope I may describe the right hon. gentleman who leads the opposition-

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext: I am honoured.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext: -and to my colleague the Minister of Justice my thanks for their appreciative words. I think I have known the leader of the opposition for a greater number of years than I have known even the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext: Oh, yes; I was on the platform with the hon. gentleman for the union government, although I was not a candidate.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext: If my right hon. friend will search his memory a little more closely, I think he will find that he was not on the platform with me in 1917, but at any rate we were fighting on the same side at that time.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext: Yes; I was on the platform with the hon. gentleman at Calgary.

subtopic: BIRTHDAY GREETINGS TO HON. T. A. CRERAR
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice has alluded to my earlier appearance in this house, and to the speech he made on one occasion. I was really so enamoured of the very pleasant personality of the minister, even when he was in opposition, that I could not resist smiling across the gangway at him.
I do wish to express my thanks to the members of the house who are still here at this late hour for the very kind way in which they have received the altogether too generous felicitations of my colleague and the right hon. leader of the opposition. Sixty-two years is getting well along in the allotted span, but I hope I may have still a few years of useful service before me. During the next year or two, at any rate, which will constitute the term of this parliament, I hope I may have an opportunity to acquire wisdom from both *the leader of the opposition and the Minister of Justice.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
